item.title: Japan's economic foundation undercut by defense spending
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:34:00
China Japan Photo: GT The Japanese government is considering a plan to increase corporate tax to fund a boost in defense spending, Japan Today reported on Sunday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The business community, however, may resist a corporate tax increase out of concern that it could hamper wage hikes and undermine Japan's international competitiveness, the report said. It wasn't long ago that the Japanese government imposed a defense surtax on companies. In March 2025, Japan introduced the 2025 Tax Reform Law and Regulations, effective April 1, 2026, which includes a 4 percent special defense surtax imposed on corporate income tax. The fact that another tax increase is being floated just months later suggests that the funding from the previous measure is already insufficient to satisfy the appetite for more defense spending - and this is happening against a backdrop of extremely fragile public finances. There is no shortage of data reflecting the fragility of the ground on which its fiscal policy stands. Japan's debt, more than twice the size of its economy, faces upward pressure due to rising social security, national defense and debt-servicing costs. Its total outstanding debt hit a record high of 1,342.17 trillion yen ($8.6 trillion) at the end of 2025, according to data from the country's Finance Ministry. Even more fundamental pressure comes from its demographic structure. Japan has the highest proportion of people age 65 and older among 39 countries with populations of at least 40 million people. The number of people age 65 and older stood at an estimated 36.24 million as of September 15, accounting for 29.6 percent of the country's total, the highest percentage on record. Such a large elderly population implies massive social security spending which, together with debt service costs, has left Japan with almost no fiscal room for maneuver. Beyond the fiscal predicament, Japan's current economy offers little cushion. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Japanese household spending fell 3.1 percent year-on-year in August - the ninth consecutive monthly decline. Yields on Japanese government bonds this year have climbed to multi-decade highs, while the yen has weakened to its lowest level since 1986. Wholesale prices rose 6.8 percent in the year to September, slowing from the previous month but underscoring mounting inflationary pressure that keeps alive market expectations of a near-term rate hike. The persistent downward pressure on the yen has not eased, and the high cost of imported energy and raw materials has already drastically squeezed the profit margins of a large number of manufacturers and small and medium-sized services enterprises. Against this backdrop, the Japanese government has ignored these fiscal and economic strains and kept pushing defense spending higher. The defense budget for fiscal 2026 has crossed the mark of 9 trillion yen for the first time in history, setting a new record. Japan is reportedly working to revise three key security policy documents by year-end, which would likely push annual defense outlays above 10 trillion yen. However, targeting the corporate sector for more tax revenue runs essentially counter to the government's own industrial policy goals. The corporate tax base is deeply connected to investment, employment, wage growth and industrial competitiveness, especially at a moment when Japan is trying to maintain its foothold in key sectors such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence and new energy. Japanese enterprises are already operating under high pressure. Yen depreciation has driven up import costs, labor shortages have pushed up labor expenses, and competition in the global industrial chain has grown increasingly fierce. If the corporate tax is raised further, the funds that companies had planned to use for raising salaries, investing in technological research and development, and upgrading production equipment will all be siphoned off to cover military spending. The end result will only be a further decline in corporate competitiveness, stagnant incomes for workers, and an already weak recovery in private consumption losing even more of its supporting foundation. Funding military expansion through tax hikes would squeeze Japan's financial situation and inject new uncertainty into the regional security situation. A country that keeps paying for its military buildup with tax increases will only push itself and the entire region into a far more costly confrontation. In the end, the path that erodes its own economic foundation is destined to be unsustainable.

item.title: China's Q3 economic data conveys confidence to a turbulent world: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:28:00
Technicians debug robots installed on the new production line at a welding workshop in Yiwu, East China's Zhejiang Province, on February 25, 2026. Photo: VCG Amid a complex and volatile external environment, China's economy has withstood headwinds and maintained steady performance, conveying confidence and certainty to a turbulent world. The stable growth of the Chinese economy provides strong safeguards for the resilience and smooth operation of global supply chains. It is injecting new momentum into the global economy and providing solid support for global demand and supply. On Monday, China's National Bureau of Statistics released the closely watched third-quarter economic data: In the first three quarters of this year, China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 4.6 per cent year-on-year, with growth of 4.5 per cent in the third quarter, continuing to demonstrate the resilience and vitality of the economy. Foreign media widely described the outcome as "beating estimates" or "beating expectations." Agence France-Presse (AFP) noted that the Chinese economy "is under pressure" from soaring energy costs caused by geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East. Amid such a complex and volatile external environment, China's economy has withstood headwinds and maintained steady performance, conveying confidence and certainty to a turbulent world. Amid diverging growth trends among the world's major economies and rising uncertainty, the Chinese economy - as the world's second-largest - has maintained stable performance, serving as a "ballast" for the global economy. At present, the international supply and demand system is undergoing a profound reshaping; global energy supplies remain tight, and prices for various industrial raw materials have risen sharply. In this context, in the first three quarters, the value-added output of industrial enterprises above designated size nationwide grew by 5.3 per cent year-on-year, with value-added output in high-tech manufacturing rising by 14.3 per cent, 9 percentage points faster than the growth rate for all industrial enterprises above designated size. China's industrial production remains generally stable and resilient, helping to cushion the transmission of external shocks and reduce the risk of global economic volatility. The stable growth of the Chinese economy provides strong safeguards for the resilience and smooth operation of global supply chains. As the world's manufacturing hub and a key supplier of intermediate goods, China's industrial and supply chains are deeply integrated into the global economy. The smooth operation on the production side and sustained growth in industry have ensured a stable supply of key products, components and raw materials to global markets. On the policy front, the continued promotion of high-level opening-up, the optimization of the business environment and the facilitation of trade have further consolidated China's role as a global supply chain hub. At a time when global supply chains face mounting restructuring pressures, the stable operation of the Chinese economy has effectively reduced the risks of supply chain disruptions and bottlenecks, providing a reliable guarantee for the stable production and trade activities of enterprises worldwide. Some foreign media outlets believe that the boom in artificial intelligence exports has driven the growth of China's economy. China's ever-expanding new quality productive forces have not only driven the national economy towards a development trajectory characterized by renewed momentum and an optimized structure, but are also injecting new momentum into the global economy. In the first three quarters, output of products such as 3D printing equipment, lithium-ion batteries and industrial robots maintained rapid growth, whilst new drivers such as green and low-carbon development, the digital economy and smart manufacturing continued to gain strength. These advances have not only driven the optimization and upgrading of China's domestic industrial structure but have also provided technological, product and market opportunities for the global industrial and value chains to transition towards high-end, intelligent and green development, assisting the global community in tackling climate change and promoting sustainable development. Data on China's imports and exports for the first three quarters, released by the General Administration of Customs on October 14, showed that China's imports grew by 22.3 percent, outpacing export growth. This indicates that the Chinese market continues to demonstrate a strong capacity to absorb goods from around the world. The upcoming China International Import Expo (CIIE) will attract more than 4,100 overseas companies, bringing more new products, technologies and services from across the globe to the Chinese market. China's efforts to expand opening-up are reflected not only in its products and investments going global, but also in its proactive efforts to share market opportunities with the rest of the world. Some foreign media outlets frequently focus on "trade deficits" when interpreting China's foreign trade data. Yet the figures for the first three quarters show that, as a vast, open market with a stable economy, China continues to generate orders for businesses worldwide, serving as a driving force for global trade. At present, the potential of China's domestic market still needs to be further unlocked, and the foundation for sustained economic improvement needs to be consolidated. Nevertheless, positive factors also deserve attention. In the first three quarters, the real growth of China's per capita disposable income of households was 4.4 percent, while the real growth of the per capita disposable income of rural households was 5.6 percent. Total retail sales of consumer goods and services rose by 2.6 per cent year-on-year. Search entries for the "China Haul" phenomenon keep hitting new highs. From January to August, the number of visa-free inbound foreign visitors rose 26.8% year-on-year, and tax-refund spending upon departure has surged across many regions. These trends illustrate how China's high-quality products, consumer experiences, convenient services and stable domestic demand are providing solid support for global demand and supply. China's economic report card for the first three quarters not only reflects the country's progress in high-quality development, but also provides valuable confidence and certainty for the global economy. What the world can see from these figures is that, by strengthening its supply-side foundations through innovation, enhancing growth resilience through domestic demand, and expanding opportunities for cooperation through opening-up, China's economy is transforming its current growth resilience into a long-term initiative in development, while creating more opportunities for the rest of the world.

item.title: China urges UK not to follow EU lead on EV restrictions, vows countermeasures if restrictions imposed: MOFCOM
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:04:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG A spokesperson from China's Ministry of Commerce on Monday urged the UK to abide by WTO rules, exercise caution and avoid simply following the EU's approach, stressing that China will closely monitor relevant developments, when commenting on reports that UK Trade Minister Anas Sarwar claimed Britain and the European Union must "work together and act in lockstep" to address China's dominance in the auto industry and was still discussing possible additional tariffs on Chinese EVs with European partners. China-UK cooperation in the auto industry is complementary, equal and mutually beneficial, the spokesperson said. If the UK insists on imposing restrictive measures on Chinese electric vehicles, China will take resolute countermeasures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries. Global Times

item.title: Chinese FM, diplomatic missions in France urge Chinese nationals to step up safety precautions amid nationwide protests
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:00:00
Riot police stand amid debris and smoke on a street in Paris, France, on October 18, 2026, following large-scale demonstrations the previous day. Photo: VCG China's Foreign Ministry and Chinese diplomatic missions in France have once again urged Chinese nationals planning to travel to France to remain alert to potential risks, closely monitor local developments, strengthen safety precautions and avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place, China Central Television (CCTV) News reported on Monday. Large-scale demonstrations have erupted in dozens of cities across France, including Paris, Marseille and Lyon, with some protests turning violent and clashes breaking out between demonstrators and police. In the event of an emergency, Chinese nationals are advised to contact local police promptly and seek assistance from Chinese diplomatic missions in France, according to CCTV News. Ahead of the demonstrations, the Chinese Embassy and consulates in France issued a notice on Friday, warning that large-scale protests involving trade unions and student groups were expected to take place across France on Saturday. The notice urged Chinese nationals in France, particularly tourists, to remain vigilant, closely monitor local developments, avoid protest areas and take necessary safety precautions. Global Times

item.title: US-Japan drills lay bare true meaning of Japan's 'exclusive defense' narrative
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 20:45:00
Representatives of groups opposing the upcoming Japan-US joint military exercise Keen Sword 27, along with prefectural assembly members, submit a petition addressed to Oita Governor Sato on October 15, 2026 at the prefectural government office, calling for the cancellation of the exercise scheduled to begin on October 19, 2026. Photo: Screenshot of Oita Asahi Broadcasting If a force repeatedly insists that it is acting in self-defense, perhaps the best way to judge is not its press releases, but where it places its missiles. According to Japanese media, US-Japan Keen Sword 27 military exercises - "seen as a dress rehearsal for defending Japan's southwestern island chain" - kicked off Monday. This year's exercise is the largest of its kind to date. But what is this "sword" really for? The answer is not in the exercise's introduction, but in a string of firsts. The first "first": The drill will see Japan for the first time deploy its longer-range Type 25 surface-to-ship missiles outside their base in Kumamoto Prefecture. It derived from the Type 12 anti-ship missile. As its name may have maintained understated, its reported range has surged from roughly 200 kilometers to 1,000 kilometers. Reports say the range puts much of the East China Sea, parts of China's coast and the Korean Peninsula within reach. This is no longer simply a defensive system. With its extended range, it substantially increases Japan's ability to conduct long-range strikes. Deploying it in a major exercise is a clear indication that Japan's military is expanding. The second "first": The US' NMESIS anti-ship missile system will be deployed to Yonaguni Island, barely 110 km from Taiwan island, for the first time. Though marketed as an anti-ship system, NMESIS can fire cruise missile Naval Strike Missile, which provides precision land-attack capabilities. It means a once-quiet maritime outpost is being turned into a forward military position capable of launching strikes The third "first": Five countries - France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines - will join the exercise for the first time. The drills let Washington show it can still rally partners in the Western Pacific, while giving Tokyo a chance to wrap its expanding military role - and its move away from exclusive defense - in the appearance of allied consent. The fourth "first": The exercise is expanding further into emerging domains of warfare. Alongside traditional drills involving integrated air and missile defense and ground operations training, the exercise also includes cyberattack response, information warfare training and electromagnetic warfare training. It signals Japan's drive to enhance its abilities in emerging domains of warfare and deepen the "modernization" of the US-Japan alliance. Nevertheless, a country committed to exclusively defense-oriented policy has little reason to rehearse 1,000-kilometer missiles strikes, or to station offensive-capable weapons on small islands sitting right next to its neighbors. These steps indicate that the US and Japan are moving past conventional island defense, converting Japan's southwestern islands into forward nodes for projecting power outward. The region is concerned not simply because the exercise is larger, but because Japan's placement of weapons is changing what "defense" means in practice. Japan's ambitions pose longer-term risks. It seems to be using joint drills to steadily erode the limits of exclusive defense, after all, 1,000-km missiles far exceed any narrow territorial requirement. At the same time, it is trying to integrate more deeply into US operations, moving from a protected ally toward a core role in the forward posture along the First Island Chain. These efforts also align with Tokyo's wider push to revise the pacifist constitution. Taken together, they raise serious questions about where Japan's postwar security identity is heading. European participants are largely symbolic. They may be willing to appear in an exercise, but that does not mean they are prepared to bear the heavy costs of a conflict in the Western Pacific. The US, for its part, has long kept strategic ambiguity on Taiwan question. Whether Washington would fight on Japan's behalf in a crisis remains an entirely different question. As for Japan, Tokyo seems to think that tightening its alignment with Washington and acquiring offensive-capable weapons will boost its geopolitical position. Yet this overlooks a stark reality: Stationing missiles only 110 kilometers from Taiwan island would place Japan on the front line of one of the region's most volatile flashpoints if fighting broke out. Waving weapons on one's own doorstep can hardly bring lasting peace. More often, it simply stacks the risks higher and puts one closer to the flames. Japan once pursued a militarist path that brought great suffering to Asia. As it now boosts its military role again, the question is not just how much protection it says it needs, but how it will prove it will not repeat that history. When Japan's missile ranges run ahead of peace commitments, and long-range strike power quietly supplants exclusive defense, the more prominently Keen Sword is displayed, the heavier the shadow it may cast across the region.

item.title: Chinese actress cancels Bangkok fan meeting amid embassy travel safety alert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 19:15:00
Bai Lu Photo: IC Chinese actress Bai Lu on Monday canceled her fan meeting in Bangkok scheduled for Sunday, citing risk warnings following recent alleged missing, scam incidents in Thailand, and pledged to compensate eligible fans for related flight and hotel cancellation or change fees. According to a statement released by Bai’s official studio on Sina Weibo, the Meet & Love Bai Lu Special Fan Meeting, scheduled for October 25 in Bangkok, had been canceled following consultations with the platform amid recent risk warnings. Bai, whose original name is Bai Mengyan, is a Chinese actress and model born in 1994 and best known for her roles in TV series such as Untouchable Lovers , One and Only and Forever and Ever . The statement said that the fan meeting was canceled after careful assessment, with the safety of attendees and trouble-free travel arrangements identified as the studio’s and organizers’ top priorities. The statement also said that Bai and her studio offered to compensate eligible domestic and overseas fans who purchased tickets through official channels for actual flight and hotel cancellation or change fees related to the canceled Bangkok event, covering travel from October 24 to 26. The Chinese Embassy in Thailand warned last Friday that there had recently been several cases of Chinese nationals going missing, being illegally detained or being deceived into traveling onward to the Thai-Myanmar border after entering Thailand. The embassy said criminals had lured Chinese nationals to Thailand under the pretext of high-paying jobs, business visits, investment opportunities and project invitations, then subjected them to criminal acts, threatening their personal safety and property. It also warned of recent scams targeting livestreamers and performers in China with fraudulent invitations to filming and performance engagements. The Chinese Embassy in Thailand urged Chinese nationals visiting the country to stay alert to scams and take precautions to ensure their safety. Global Times

item.title: China updates UAV export controls covering 3-hour endurance, UAVs with high-capacity aerosol dispensing systems
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 16:16:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China on Monday moved to optimize export controls on a range of dual-use products, with updated measures covering certain unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and related equipment as well as dredgers, while new controls were introduced on high-end engineering equipment including tunnel boring machines and walking excavators, according to statements released by the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM). The export controls will take effect on November 18. Notably, the UAV-related adjustments tighten controls on some higher-risk items while streamlining export procedures for certain products that, with technological advances, have become widely used in civilian applications. A spokesperson for MOFCOM stressed on Monday that the items covered by the measures have clear dual-use characteristics. China's implementation of export controls in accordance with laws and regulations is consistent with common international practice, better safeguards national security and interests, and enables the country to better fulfill its international obligations, including non-proliferation commitments, the spokesperson said. Chinese experts said the adjustments reflect a broader effort to keep export-control rules aligned with technological and industrial change. As sophisticated equipment becomes more capable and widely used, closer scrutiny of buyers, end users and end uses is increasingly necessary to reduce misuse risks while preserving legitimate civilian trade and international cooperation. Targeted adjustment amid technological change According to the MOFCOM, export restrictions on certain UAV-related items cover products meeting specified technical thresholds, including autopilots, long-endurance unmanned aircraft or airships, and certain engines specially designed for such aircraft. For instance, autopilots specially designed for UAVs are among the items that may not be exported without authorization. The export controls also cover UAVs or unmanned airships capable of controlled flight beyond the operator's natural line of sight and with a maximum endurance of three hours or more. UAVs or unmanned airships with a maximum endurance of at least 30 minutes but less than three hours, and capable of taking off and maintaining stable controlled flight in wind gusts of at least 46.3 kilometers per hour, or 25 knots, are also covered. However, exporters of such items may use a streamlined procedure, obtaining an export certificate by filing the required information before each shipment. Wang Yanan, editor-in-chief of Beijing-based Aerospace Knowledge magazine, said the distinction illustrates how export control rules need to evolve alongside technological advances and expanding civilian applications. As UAV technology develops, some products that were once relatively sensitive have become increasingly common in agriculture, power inspection and other commercial scenarios, Wang said. Differentiated management can therefore help avoid unnecessarily constraining normal trade while keeping closer oversight over products with greater potential risks. The controls also cover UAVs equipped with aerosol dispensing systems or devices with a capacity exceeding 80 liters, or designed to accommodate such systems or devices and capable of autonomous flight control and navigation. Certain engines specially designed for UAVs or unmanned airships are also subject to the export controls, including air-breathing piston or rotary internal combustion engines designed for flight above 15,420 meters, aircraft engines with maximum continuous power exceeding 16 kilowatts, and turbojet engines with thrust of at least 400 newtons. Certain radio communication equipment specially designed for regulated UAVs or unmanned airships is also covered, including equipment that allows a single ground station to control more than 10 aircraft. Wang said UAVs with longer endurance, larger payload capacity and higher operating capability may pose greater risks if diverted from their declared civilian purposes. Clearer technical thresholds can therefore help strengthen end-use management and reduce the risk of misuse. The MOFCOM spokesperson said the latest optimization of China's UAV export controls is based on recent industrial and technological developments reported by the industry, reflecting China's firm opposition to drones being illegally used for non-peaceful purposes while also supporting Chinese companies in international trade and cooperation in civilian UAV applications. Balancing security and global trade Beyond UAVs, China also adjusted export controls on certain dredger-related items and introduced controls on selected high-end engineering equipment. The dredger-related measures cover slurry pumps, dragheads and cutterheads that meet specified technical thresholds, as well as key components specially designed for such pumps, while the engineering-equipment controls cover full-face tunnel boring machines and specially designed parts, certain walking excavators, and plateau-type wet shotcrete machines and related components and technologies. The measures come as Chinese tunneling and other high-end engineering equipment has gained a growing presence in overseas infrastructure projects. China exported about $793 million worth of self-propelled coal or rock cutters and tunneling machinery in 2025, according to Reuters, underscoring the country's role as an important supplier in the global tunneling equipment market. Chinese-produced tunnel boring machines account for nearly 70 percent of the global market, according to the website of provincial government of Central China's Hunan Province, reflecting how widely such equipment is now used in infrastructure construction worldwide. Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times that the equipment covered by the measures has clear dual-use characteristics and may create wider risks if improperly used. He said tightening management of such products is consistent with international export control practice and can help reduce potential spillover risks to international security and order. Export controls, he stressed, do not mean exports are prohibited altogether, but rather that they are subject to stricter and more clearly defined management. Zhou said the latest adjustment also responds to changes in the international security and trade environment. By drawing clearer boundaries around controlled products and setting more precise requirements, China can improve both the efficiency and effectiveness of export control procedures while continuing to facilitate compliant trade. He added that China's export control system is continuing to evolve based on practical experience and changing external conditions, and that the latest measures also reflect ongoing interaction and communication with relevant international partners. MOFCOM said China had notified relevant countries and regions with which it has established export control dialogue mechanisms before announcing the measures. The ministry said China is willing to work with other countries to maintain stable and smooth global industrial and supply chains, and that export license applications meeting relevant requirements will be approved.

item.title: China's Central Archives opens over 5,000 Long March items to mark 90th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 10:10:00
China's Central Archives opens more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on October 19, 2026 to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory. Photo: CCTV News China's Central Archives opened more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on Monday to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory, offering firsthand accounts of key battles, strategic decisions and solidarity between soldiers and civilians, according to state broadcaster CCTV News. The newly accessible materials mainly date from October 1934 to October 1936, including programs and declarations issued by the Communist Party of China (CPC), Red Army telegrams and reports on operational deployments, and revolutionary newspapers and periodicals founded and published by the CPC. Together, they showcase the revolutionary spirit of the CPC and the people's armed forces, vividly depicting how the Red Army and ordinary people stood united, braved sacrifice and pressed ahead during the Long March, according to CCTV News. Among the materials opened to the public for the first time is Jiebao (victory bulletin), a newspaper founded by the CPC's Shanghai central bureau. A total of 40 issues were published between October 1933 and June 1935, exposing the reactionary rule of the Kuomintang, publicizing the Red Army's military achievements and development in the revolutionary base areas. Liu Kun, a staff member of the Central Archives' archival access department, was cited as saying that "the issue of Jiebao , published on December 17, 1934, carried a report stating, 'The westward-bound Red Army has victoriously captured Liping in Guizhou' … Liping was the site of the first Political Bureau meeting held by the CPC Central Committee after the Long March had begun. The Liping Meeting affirmed the decision to change course at Tongdao and established the Red Army's strategy of advancing westward, thereby averting the risk of being encircled and annihilated by Kuomintang forces had it continued north." The words "utmost urgency" on the telegram testify to the critical military situation at the time. The words "utmost urgency" on the telegram testify to the critical military situation at the time. Another document, titled "Report on the first division's covering of the entire army's bridge crossing tomorrow," provides a detailed account of the Red Army's exploits in capturing Luding Bridge, said Liu. "The capture of Luding Bridge was one of the major victories of strategic significance during the Red Army's Long March," Liu said. "As a firsthand battlefield record, this document details when units of the First Red Army Corps arrived at Luding Bridge and launched their attacks. It also records the situation on the ground as they captured the bridge, defeated a regiment of Sichuan troops and seized military supplies. The document states, 'Today, we captured more than 100 prisoners and over 100 firearms, along with enough ammunition and hand grenades to substantially replenish our supplies.'" The 25th Red Army set out from Hejiachong in Luoshan county, Henan Province, on November 16, 1934, and arrived in Yongping, Shaanxi Province, on September 15, 1935, to become the first Red Army force to reach northern Shaanxi during the Long March. A special report submitted to the CPC Central Committee on July 17, 1935, by Wu Huanxian, the political commissar of the 25th Red Army, is an important historical source for research into the force's Long March. "In this report, Wu perceptively raised the question of whether they could join forces with the 26th and 28th armies, concentrate their strength to destroy enemy forces, support the main Red Army's operations in the northwest, and swiftly establish a new, strong and consolidated revolutionary base there," Liu said. "Operating in isolation, without instructions from the CPC Central Committee or deployments ordered by higher authorities, the CPC Hubei-Henan-Shaanxi Provincial Committee resolutely decided that the main force of the 25th Red Army should advance westward and northward to support the main Red Army. Wu's report also explains the thinking behind that decision," Liu said. Starting Monday, audiences can consult these materials at the Central Archives' public reading hall by presenting valid identification, such as a national ID card or work ID, per CCTV News. Global Times

item.title: China's GDP expands 4.6% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, on track to meet pre-set annual growth target
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 10:03:00
Photo: Li Xuanmin/Global Times China's GDP expanded 4.6 percent year-on-year to reach 107.11 trillion yuan ($16 trillion) in the first nine months, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Monday. The freshly released figure landed well within the annual GDP growth target of around 4.5 percent to 5 percent for this year, showing that the world's second-largest economy continues to operate on the sound trajectory, and laying a solid foundation for achieving the full-year growth target, Chinese analysts said. In the third quarter, China's GDP grew 4.5 percent year-on-year, accelerating from the 4.3-percent growth recorded in the second quarter. In the first quarter, China's GDP jumped 5 percent, NBS data showed. Observers said the third-quarter reading reflects multiple factors, including the manufacturing strength of China's high-tech and equipment sectors, which continued to underpin robust external demand, the strong drive from new and emerging industries, as well as the steady progress in the course of high-quality development. Amid mounting uncertainties, the steady growth of the Chinese economy - which serves as both the "world's market" and a "super buyer" - is an anchor of growth, channeling much-needed certainty to the world economy, analysts said. 'New, high-quality development' "Based on the forecasts by some international institutions, China's growth rate of 4.6 percent still leads among the world's major economies. Also, in terms of absolute increase, the Chinese economy in the first three quarters added 5.7 trillion yuan in output, the largest increment in the past five years," NBS deputy head Mao Shengyong said at a press briefing of the State Council Information Office on Monday. China's 5.7 trillion yuan increment in economic output in the first three quarters is roughly equivalent to the annual GDP of Belgium, the world's 23rd largest economy. Mao also stressed that China's third-quarter GDP growth rebounded by 0.2 percentage point from the second quarter, which is "hard-won and highly commendable," as the greater impact of higher international oil prices caused by the Middle East conflict led some international institutions to lower their third-quarter growth forecasts for major economies compared with the second quarter. "The Chinese economy demonstrated a clear trend of advancing toward new and higher-quality development in the first three quarters, with growth momentum shifting toward new drivers from old ones," Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times. "China has achieved almost the best result it can taking account of amassing downward pressures, especially the increasingly complicated geopolitical environment," he added. One of the major takeaways from the first nine months data is the continuous improvement of economic structure, as "what matters more at this stage of economic upgrade and transformation is the quality," analysts said. According to the NBS data, China's value-added industrial output of above-scale enterprises in the first nine months rose 5.3 percent compared to the same period in 2025. Meanwhile, new growth drivers continued to gain ground, with contributions to the overall economy exceeding 40 percent in the first three quarters. The value-added of high-tech manufacturing rose 14.3 percent, while equipment manufacturing grew 10.2 percent. Also, output of 3D printing equipment, lithium-ion batteries and industrial robots surged 62.5 percent, 39.5 percent and 29.1 percent, respectively. China's resilient production and relatively rapid export growth have played an important role in boosting the economy in the third quarter, especially in the manufacturing of high-tech products related to artificial intelligence (AI), chips and new-energy vehicles. "China's economic growth stems from overall optimization rather than short-term gains driven by any single indicator or policy stimulus. The reality is very different from the pessimism peddled by some foreign media, as they often cherry-pick a single indicator for one-sided interpretation, deliberately stoking market concerns," Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Monday. Full-year target In the January-September period, China's fixed-asset investment dropped by 7.2 percent year-on-year, while total retail sales of consumer goods and services expanded by 2.6 percent year-on-year, according to the NBS data. Among which, retail sales of services rose 5 percent year-on-year in the first nine months, 4 percentage points faster than that of goods. While internal demand continued to recover in the third quarter, economists pointed to more signs of improvement in September, suggesting that policy support and seasonal factors were beginning to take effect and reinforcing the economy's underlying resilience. Analysts attributed the improvement partly to the earlier timing of the Mid-Autumn Festival, which lifted spending on essential goods, alongside support from "more proactive and effective" macro policies, and a low base effect from last year. "Internally, the Chinese economy faces several challenges, including insufficient domestic demand, weak consumer confidence, and a property market downturn that continues to weigh on the recovery of fixed-asset investment. Externally, uncertainties in the Middle East and trade disputes among major economies could pose pressures on the economic outlook," Tian Yun, a Beijing-based veteran economist, told the Global Times. Despite the headwinds, observers voiced confidence that the Chinese economy will maintain strategic composure and continue to advance in a new and better direction. While the series of pro-growth policies launched since September could further stabilize and guide market expectations, more incremental policies are also expected to address modest consumption and investment in the fourth quarter - the final stretch of 2026 and a critical window for consolidating the economy's recovery and upward momentum. Observers believe that the economic operation in the first nine months has set the tone for the country to achieve the full-year GDP growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent. "The ongoing transformation toward new drives will not only improve the quality of growth and enhanced the economy's resilience and dynamics but also provided a solid buffer against external uncertainties," Tian stressed. The freshly released data also squarely rejects the pessimism some doomsayers have been spreading about the Chinese economy. In the past, China was often described as the "world's factory" and a "super seller" thanks to its strong production capacity. Now, with imports growing by more than 20 percent, China has also become the "world's market" and a "super buyer," reflecting the relatively strong comprehensive competitiveness of its industries, Mao said at the press briefing. Tian added that the set of figures has further highlighted China's positive contribution to the global economy. "In fact, China's contribution to the global market today is not simply a matter of how large a share of global GDP it accounts for. It is now the world's second-largest consumer market, indicating its important role as a major source of demand and the enormous development opportunities it offers to the world," Tian said.
